newsitem.title: FRANCE: French weekend truck ban rules could hit air cargo.
newsitem.headline: French weekend truck ban rules could hit air cargo.

text.p: Airfreight truckers said they have not been adequately informed by the French authorities of the implications of a weekend truck ban coming into effect on March 24.

Currently, truckers are allowed to return to their home locations after making deliveries. But when the new regulations come into force, vehicles weighing more than 7.5 tonnes, will banned from French roads between 2200 local (2100 gmt) on Saturday until the same time on Sunday.

The ban was one of the conditions laid down in the agreement signed by French truckers' unions, road haulage companies and the government at the end of 1996 to resolve a 12-day lorry drivers' dispute.

The only major exemptions from the ban are perishable shipments, live animals and printed matter. In all other cases, trucking companies will have to seek special permits from France's prefectoral authorities which are responsible for enforcement of road traffic regulations in the country's departments.

"Frankly, we have been left in the dark on this ban and the transport ministry simply does not realise the important role trucking plays in airfreight, especially during weekend periods," said Joelle Bruel.

Bruel is transport manager of Road Flight Systems(RFS) -- based at Paris-Charles de Gaulle airport -- which specialises in European trucking services on behalf of a number of airlines including the Air France group.

She added: "Air France contacted us recently on new proposed trucking routes operating Sundays with the introduction of summer schedules. However, we warned them of the difficulties which might arise due to the truck ban.
"It's likely they'll be taking up the issue with government officials but we do not expect a clarification of the situation before the ban takes effect," Bruel said.

On routes from France, RFS vehicles operate under special permits during the weekend periods in question for the transport of freight which does not fall into the exemption categories. Several of these permits expire in October 1997.

"While there is uncertainty over the renewal of these permits, a more immediate problem is whether we will be able to maintain our inbound routes to Paris from major EU routes which until now have been free of restriction because they concern trucks returning home."

She added: "If the ban is applied to the letter then everyone in the air cargo industry is going to have to make an enormous effort at re-adapting themselves to what will be a radically different logistics time-frame."
Another French airfreight trucking company, Airliner, also complained at the lack of clear guidelines on the new regulations.

"We're in limbo at the moment and there's a real fear we will no longer be in a position to serve airlines during what is a vital trucking period, not to mention the knock-on effect on flight schedules," an Airliner official said.

"As usual, France has been too keen to introduce EU directives while other countries continue to take a more liberal view and in Germany, operators have the possibility of buying permits. There is thus a danger that where possible airlines will by-pass French airports, re-routing to other gateways such as Brussels and Amsterdam," an Airliner official said.
Already, special permits had become more difficult to obtain from the prefectures, the official added.

"Before, it was common to have long-term permits for up to one year but now it's more and more the case that these are issued for shorter durations, two to three months only, for example. Moreover, one finds that a prefect in one region takes a more flexible line than others. Overall, it's become an unpredictable process."
One fear among foreign hauliers operating from France is that they will be discriminated against vis a vis their French counterparts.

"We just don't know how many permits, if any, will be issued after March 24 and whether any distinction will be made between French- and foreign-registered vehicles. The prefecture we contacted recently was just not capable of giving us any clear information. It's a mess," another Paris-CDG operator told Reuters.
A transport ministry official said provision was made under the new regulations for freight which was deemed "absolutely urgent."
"However, let's be clear: operators would have to demonstrate that shipments did fall into this category and it would then be left to the prefect's discretion to validate the request or not."
Dutch airline KLM Royal Netherlands Airline NV has already taken measures to get around the truck ban.

Last month, it tested out a week-end freighter service from Zaragoza to Amsterdam, using a 30 tonne-capacity Belfast aircraft in anticipation of the ban affecting its trucking operations on the route.
The airline is also considering a similar operation between Italy and Schiphol.
